facts.fact: An ecosystem is biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) plus abiotic parts acting as one unit.
Energy flow is one-way; Lindeman's 10% law passes about 10% to the next trophic level.
The pyramid of energy is always upright; number and biomass pyramids can invert.
Grazing food chains start with green plants; detritus chains with dead matter.
Food chains rarely exceed 4–5 links because of energy loss.
Biodiversity has three levels: genetic, species and ecosystem.
India is one of 17 megadiverse countries: about 2.4% of land, about 8% of species.
A hotspot needs at least 1,500 endemic plants AND 70% loss of primary vegetation.
Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Sundaland.
Cerrado (Brazil) is a hotspot that does NOT extend into India.
The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 is the umbrella law passed after Bhopal (1984).
The Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 has four schedules after the 2022 amendment; Schedule I is highest protection.
The National Board for Wildlife is chaired by the Prime Minister.
The Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 was renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023.
The National Biodiversity Authority is in Chennai.
The Water Act 1974 created the CPCB/SPCBs; the Air Act came in 1981; NGT in 2010.
National Parks allow no rights or grazing; sanctuaries may allow regulated rights.
Conservation reserves are government land near PAs; community reserves are community land.
Project Tiger 1973; NTCA 2005; 58 tiger reserves (2025); 3,682 tigers (2022).
Project Cheetah (2022) brought African cheetahs to Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh.
Project Elephant began in 1992.
ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76%, forest + tree cover 25.17%.
ISFR forest cover = land of 1 ha or more with canopy density of 10% or more.
Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (Nallamala) is India's largest tiger reserve.
Coringa (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove formation.
Pulicat is India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon (after Chilika).
Kolleru is AP's only Ramsar site (2002) and a wildlife sanctuary (1999).
Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve.
Rollapadu WLS protects the Great Indian Bustard.
Red sanders is endemic to the southern Eastern Ghats, IUCN Endangered and CITES-listed.
Kolleru = Ramsar + WPA; NSTR = Project Tiger/NTCA; Seshachalam = UNESCO MAB; Coringa = WPA sanctuary.
The Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; India joined in 1982.
India had 103 Ramsar sites by October 2026; Tamil Nadu has the most.
The Montreux Record lists threatened Ramsar sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
Biosphere reserves follow UNESCO MAB (1971), zoned core, buffer and transition; India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first.
12 Indian biosphere reserves are on the UNESCO World Network.
CITES (1973) controls trade; CMS (Bonn, 1979) protects migratory species; India hosted CMS COP13 (Gandhinagar, 2020).
Olive Ridley: IUCN Vulnerable, CITES Appendix I, WPA Schedule I, mass nesting 'arribada'.
Main GHGs include CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs and SF6 (highest GWP).
The IPCC was set up by WMO and UNEP in 1988; it assesses, not conducts, science.
UNFCCC (Rio 1992) is the parent; Kyoto (1997) bound developed nations; Paris (2015) uses NDCs.
The Paris Agreement aims for well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C.
COP27 (2022, Sharm el-Sheikh) created the Loss and Damage Fund.
COP28 (2023, Dubai) held the first Global Stocktake.
COP30 was held at Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.
Panchamrit: 500 GW non-fossil, 50% RE, 1 bn t CO2 cut, 45% intensity cut by 2030, net-zero 2070.
NAPCC (2008) has eight missions; states have SAPCCs.
Mission LiFE (2022) promotes pro-planet lifestyles; it is not a NAPCC mission.
ISA and CDRI are India-initiated global coalitions.
NCAP (2019) cuts particulates, tracked by the six-band AQI; single-use plastic banned from 1 July 2022.
The DM Act 2005 created NDMA (chaired by PM) and NDRF; India follows Sendai 2015-30.
Sulphate-aerosol injection and cirrus thinning are geoengineering to reduce global warming.
Carbon fertilization = more plant growth from higher CO2.
Remote sensing can measure chlorophyll, paddy GHG emissions and land-surface temperature.
Neem-coated urea slows urea dissolution in soil.
Acid rain = SO2 + NOx; photochemical smog = NOx + VOCs + sunlight → O3 and PAN.
Excess N fertiliser raises soil acidity and leaches nitrate — it does not boost N-fixers.
BPA is a component of polycarbonate plastic and an endocrine disruptor.
Benzene is a VOC from exhaust, tobacco smoke and wood burning.
Decomposers are fungi and bacteria, not viruses.
Coral–zooxanthellae and lichen (fungus + alga) are mutualisms.
Sea cow and sea lion are mammals; the sea horse is a fish.
Stockholm Conference: 1972 — created UNEP; World Environment Day 5 June.
Brundtland Report ("Our Common Future"): 1987 — defined sustainable development.
Rio Earth Summit: 1992 — Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD.
Vienna Convention: 1985 — framework for protecting the ozone layer.
Montreal Protocol: 1987 — phases out ozone-depleting CFCs; the first treaty ratified by every UN member.
Kigali Amendment: 2016 — phases down HFCs; India by 85% between 2032 and 2047.
Basel Convention: 1989 — transboundary movement of hazardous wastes.
Rotterdam Convention: 1998 — prior informed consent for trade in hazardous chemicals.
Stockholm Convention: 2001 — persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as DDT.
Minamata Convention: 2013 — mercury pollution.
UNCCD: 1994 — desertification; India hosted COP14 at Greater Noida (2019).
Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework: CBD COP15, December 2022 — 23 targets incl. 30x30 (protect 30% of land and sea by 2030).
CBD COP16 (Cali, Colombia, 2024): set up the Cali Fund for benefits from digital sequence information.
High Seas (BBNJ) Treaty: adopted 2023; entered into force January 2026 — marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction.
International Whaling Commission: 1946 — moratorium on commercial whaling since 1986.
COP1 (Berlin, 1995): first Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC.
COP3 (Kyoto, 1997): Kyoto Protocol — binding cuts for developed countries; CDM carbon credits.
COP8 (New Delhi, 2002): the climate COP hosted by India — Delhi Declaration.
COP15 (Copenhagen, 2009): Copenhagen Accord — US$100 billion a year climate-finance pledge.
COP16 (Cancún, 2010): set up the Green Climate Fund.
COP21 (Paris, 2015): Paris Agreement; International Solar Alliance launched.
COP26 (Glasgow, 2021): Glasgow Climate Pact — coal 'phase down'; India's Panchamrit.
COP29 (Baku, 2024): New Collective Quantified Goal — at least US$300 billion a year by 2035; Article 6 carbon-market rules.
COP30 (Belém, November 2025): held in the Amazon; launched the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.
COP31 (Antalya, Türkiye, 9–20 November 2026): hosted by Türkiye with Australia presiding over the negotiations.
PM2.5: fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres — reach deep into the lungs.
GRAP: Graded Response Action Plan for Delhi-NCR, enforced by the Commission for Air Quality Management (2021).
BOD (biochemical oxygen demand): oxygen needed by microbes to break down organic waste — high BOD = more polluted water.
Dissolved oxygen (DO): falls as pollution rises; fish die when it is too low.
Biomagnification: rise in concentration of a poison (e.g. DDT) at each higher trophic level.
Minamata disease: mercury poisoning from contaminated fish (Japan).
Itai-itai disease: cadmium poisoning (Japan) — painful bones.
Blue-baby syndrome: nitrate in drinking water reduces oxygen in infants' blood.
Arsenic poisoning: arsenic-rich groundwater in West Bengal and Bihar.
Dobson unit: unit for measuring ozone in the atmosphere.
Ozone hole: CFC-driven thinning of stratospheric ozone, worst over Antarctica.
Ground-level ozone: a harmful pollutant formed in photochemical smog (good up high, bad nearby).
Bhopal gas tragedy (2–3 December 1984): leak of methyl isocyanate (MIC) from the Union Carbide plant.
Algal bloom: explosive algae growth from excess N and P (eutrophication), causing "dead zones".
Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016: segregation at source into wet, dry and hazardous waste.
Plastic Waste Management Rules (amended 2021–22): carry bags must be at least 120 microns (from December 2022); EPR for producers.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022: producers meet EPR recycling targets through registered recyclers.
Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022: EPR for all battery types, including EV batteries.
Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016: colour-coded bags: yellow, red, white (translucent) and blue.
CRZ Notification, 2019: Coastal Regulation Zone — limits building near the high-tide line.
EIA Notification, 2006: Environmental Impact Assessment required before clearing listed projects.
Green Credit Programme (October 2023): market-based credits for actions such as tree planting and water conservation.
Namami Gange (2014): integrated mission to clean and conserve the Ganga.
MISHTI (2023): Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes — mangrove planting.
Amrit Dharohar (2023): scheme to conserve Ramsar wetlands and promote eco-tourism.
Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam (June 2024): tree-planting campaign launched on World Environment Day.
Green India Mission: NAPCC mission to increase forest and tree cover.
National Green Tribunal: principal bench New Delhi; zonal benches Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai.
IUCN: founded 1948, HQ Gland, Switzerland — publishes the Red List.
Red List categories (safest → gone): Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct.
Great Indian Bustard: Critically Endangered — Desert NP (Rajasthan); historically Rollapadu (AP); power lines a key threat.
Gharial: Critically Endangered fish-eating crocodile — National Chambal Sanctuary.
Jerdon's courser: Critically Endangered bird rediscovered in 1986 near Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa, AP).
Vultures and diclofenac: veterinary diclofenac caused a crash; banned for animals in 2006.
Ganges river dolphin: national aquatic animal (2009); Endangered; Project Dolphin.
Elephant: declared national heritage animal in 2010.
One-horned rhinoceros: Vulnerable; most live in Kaziranga NP (Assam).
Asiatic lion: only wild population in the Gir landscape, Gujarat — 891 in 2025.
Elephant count (2025): 22,446 — first DNA-based all-India estimate.
Snow leopard: 718 in India (first national estimate, 2024); Vulnerable.
Cheetah: declared extinct in India in 1952.
Hangul (Kashmir stag): Kashmir red deer found mainly in Dachigam NP (J&K).
Sangai (brow-antlered deer): lives only on the floating Keibul Lamjao NP, Loktak Lake (Manipur).
Lion-tailed macaque: endemic primate of the Western Ghats — Silent Valley.
Project Crocodile: 1975 — began at Bhitarkanika (Odisha).
Project Snow Leopard: 2009 — high-altitude Himalayan conservation.
Project Dolphin: announced 2020 — river and marine dolphins.
Project Tiger start: 1973 with nine tiger reserves (first: Jim Corbett).
58th tiger reserve: Madhav (Madhya Pradesh), March 2025.
GIB conservation breeding: Jaisalmer centre (Rajasthan) under the Great Indian Bustard programme.
Jim Corbett NP (Uttarakhand): India's first national park — 1936, as Hailey National Park.
Hemis NP (Ladakh): India's largest national park — snow leopards.
Keibul Lamjao NP (Manipur): the world's only floating national park, on Loktak Lake.
Gir NP (Gujarat): only home of the Asiatic lion.
First Indian Ramsar sites: Chilika (Odisha) and Keoladeo (Rajasthan), 1 October 1981.
Largest Ramsar site in India: Sundarban Wetland, West Bengal (about 4,230 km²).
Natural World Heritage Sites: Kaziranga, Keoladeo, Manas, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi & Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats, Great Himalayan NP; Khangchendzonga (mixed).
Coral reefs of India: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar.
Gadgil (WGEEP, 2011) vs Kasturirangan (2013): about 64% vs about 37% of the Western Ghats as ecologically sensitive.
Eco-Sensitive Zone: buffer of up to 10 km around a protected area by default.
Mangroves (ISFR 2023): West Bengal has the most, then Gujarat.
Khejarli sacrifice (1730): Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois died protecting khejri trees (Rajasthan).
Chipko (1973): tree-hugging movement in Uttarakhand — Gaura Devi, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt.
Appiko (1983): Karnataka's version of Chipko — Panduranga Hegde.
Save Silent Valley: Kerala campaign that stopped a hydro dam; Silent Valley became a NP (1984).
Narmada Bachao Andolan: Medha Patkar and Baba Amte against large Narmada dams (Sardar Sarovar).
Jungle Bachao Andolan: tribal movement in Jharkhand (then Bihar) against teak plantations replacing sal.
AP state symbols (2018): animal blackbuck; bird rose-ringed parakeet; tree neem; flower jasmine.
Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary: breeding site of the spot-billed pelican, near Pulicat.
Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa): habitat of the Critically Endangered Jerdon's courser.
Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary: mangrove sanctuary in the Krishna estuary.
Kambalakonda WLS: Eastern Ghats forest sanctuary at Visakhapatnam.
AP forest cover (ISFR 2023): about 29,784 km² — about 18.3% of the state, below the national 21.76%.
Nallamala hills: Eastern Ghats range holding the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve and red sanders.
Ramsar sites reported on 15 October 2026: Sauj Jheel (UP) and Sukhna Lake (Chandigarh) — 102nd and 103rd.
Olive Ridley on the AP coast: nests on AP beaches such as those of Srikakulam and Visakhapatnam.
